script.opening: "Hi, it’s about my little boy Reuben. Every time he gets a cold he goes all wheezy and chesty — this is the fourth time this winter. A&E gave him the blue inhaler last time and it helped. My question really is: has he got asthma? My sister’s lad is on a brown preventer inhaler and I’m wondering if Reuben should be too. And honestly, half the time I’m not sure I’m even getting the inhaler into him properly."

facts.text: If explored: wheeze/cough ONLY with viral colds, completely well and symptom-free between episodes, no interval symptoms (no night cough or exercise/play wheeze when well), age 2. This is the classic picture of episodic VIRAL-INDUCED WHEEZE, not (yet) diagnosable as asthma — a label generally avoided this young without interval/atopic features (NICE NG245: under 5s are treated on clinical judgement with regular review; objective tests are attempted from age 5).

If assessed: currently mild — feeding/talking/playing, no marked recession or tracheal tug at rest, not distressed, sats presumably fine. Safety-net for the features that would mean urgent review (working hard to breathe, not feeding, drowsy, blue, salbutamol not lasting).

HIDDEN AGENDA — the father carries GUILT about his smoking: he half-knows it’s contributing, feels judged, and the "is it asthma / should he be on a preventer" is partly a wish to fix it with a medicine instead of facing the smoking. He may also be anxious because his own childhood asthma was frightening. The smoking and the guilt need handling without shaming, or he’ll disengage.

He struggles to give the inhaler — likely poor spacer/mask technique (not held to the face, not enough breaths, no spacer, or pressing multiple puffs). Inhaler technique with a spacer and mask is the highest-yield practical intervention and is being missed.

Officially: a yes/no on asthma and possibly a preventer inhaler. What is needed: explanation of viral-induced wheeze vs asthma (and why a preventer isn’t automatically indicated), correct spacer/mask coaching, a written action plan, smoking-cessation support offered without shame, and clear safety-netting.

ice.ideas: Reuben probably has asthma (like his cousin) and should be on a brown preventer inhaler.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — guilt about his smoking contributing (and feeling judged), plus anxiety from his own frightening childhood asthma; hoping a preventer inhaler fixes it instead of facing the smoking.
ice.expectations: A diagnosis and a preventer inhaler. What is actually needed: explanation of viral wheeze vs asthma, correct inhaler/spacer technique, an action plan, non-judgemental smoking support, and safety-netting.

cues: "Only wheezes with colds, fine in between" — episodic viral wheeze, not interval asthma; shapes whether a preventer is indicated.
"Not sure I’m getting the inhaler into him properly" — technique is the highest-yield fix and is being flagged.
Mentions trying to smoke outside / sister’s child on a preventer — the smoking guilt and the medicine-instead-of-facing-it wish.

checkpoints.text: Distinguishes EPISODIC VIRAL-INDUCED WHEEZE (wheeze only with colds, symptom-free between, very young) from asthma (interval symptoms, nocturnal/exertional, atopy), and explains why an asthma label and a regular preventer are generally not applied at this age without interval/atopic features (NICE NG245, 2024, joint with BTS and SIGN: under 5s with suspected asthma are treated on clinical judgement; an 8 to 12 week trial of twice-daily paediatric low-dose ICS is considered only when symptoms suggest a need for maintenance therapy or there are severe acute episodes)

Assesses current severity by phone and safety-nets it: feeding, talking/playing, work of breathing (recession, tracheal tug), colour, alertness, and salbutamol response/duration — knows what would mean urgent/emergency review

Optimises the ACUTE management correctly: salbutamol via a SPACER with a face mask (BTS/SIGN 158, 2019: the preferred option for mild to moderate acute wheeze in children; not nebuliser routinely), correct dosing/frequency (per BNFC and the written plan), and a clear when-to-step-up/when-to-seek-help plan — rather than reflexively starting an inhaled steroid

Identifies and corrects the INHALER TECHNIQUE problem: coaches spacer + mask use (seal on the face, one puff at a time, tidal breaths/multiple breaths per puff), recognising this is the highest-yield practical intervention; arranges a technique check

Addresses the SMOKING as a major modifiable trigger without shaming: offers smoking-cessation support (NICE NG209: very brief advice, advice not to smoke in the home or around children, referral to local stop-smoking support), explains second/third-hand smoke worsens wheeze, and frames it as the most powerful thing he can do for Reuben’s chest
Hears the guilt and anxiety beneath the asthma question; handles the smoking with compassion not judgement, and validates his own frightening childhood-asthma experience, so he stays engaged
Partners with him on a plan and checks understanding (teach-back of inhaler technique), rather than just issuing instructions

Safety-nets and follows up: a written action plan, exactly when to give salbutamol and when to seek urgent help (increased work of breathing, not feeding, drowsy, blue, reliever not lasting 4 hours → 999/ED), smoking-cessation referral, and a technique/review appointment

worked.txt: "From what you describe — wheezy only when he’s got a cold, and completely fine, running around, in between — that’s what we call viral wheeze. Lots of little ones get it because their airways are small; their colds go to the chest. The good news is most grow out of it by school age."

"On the asthma question: at two, with symptoms only during colds and nothing in between, we usually don’t label it asthma yet or put him on a daily preventer — that’s really for children who get symptoms between colds too, like night-time coughing or wheezing when they play. We watch the pattern. If interval symptoms appear, we rethink. So your instinct to ask was right, even if the answer is ‘not a preventer for now’."

"Honestly, the most useful thing today is the bit you flagged — getting the inhaler in. With a toddler it’s the blue inhaler through a spacer with a mask: seal the mask gently over his nose and mouth, ONE puff into the spacer, then let him take five or six normal breaths from it, then the next puff. Not several puffs at once. Done well, a spacer works as well as the machines in A&E. Shall I watch you do it, or book a nurse to check?"

"Can I raise something gently, and I’m not here to give you a hard time? Smoke — even smoking outside, on clothes and breath — is one of the biggest things that tips these little airways into wheeze. I say it because stopping would do more for Reuben’s chest than almost any inhaler. I’d really like to help you with that properly, no judgement, whenever you’re ready."

"And — your own asthma as a kid sounded frightening. It makes total sense you’re watchful with Reuben. The difference is we can give you a clear plan so you’re never guessing in the middle of the night."

"So: I’ll give you a written plan. When he’s wheezy with a cold, the blue inhaler through the spacer, this dose, this often. Get urgent help — 999 or A&E — if he’s working hard to breathe with his ribs sucking in, can’t feed or talk, goes drowsy or blue, or the inhaler doesn’t last four hours. Right now he sounds mild. Let’s book a technique check and a review, and sort the smoking support. You’re doing a good job — let’s make it easier."

f.learning: Episodic viral-induced wheeze (wheeze only with colds, symptom-free between, very young child) is distinct from asthma and generally does NOT warrant an asthma label or a regular inhaled-steroid preventer at age 2 without interval or atopic features — the right answer to "should he be on a brown inhaler?" is often a well-explained "not for now" (NICE NG245: an 8 to 12 week ICS trial is considered only when symptoms suggest a need for maintenance therapy or there are severe acute episodes). The highest-yield practical intervention is INHALER TECHNIQUE: salbutamol via a spacer with a face mask (one puff, several tidal breaths, good seal), which works as well as a nebuliser when done correctly and which the father flagged he was getting wrong. The examinable hidden agenda is parental guilt about smoking (and feeling judged) plus anxiety from his own childhood asthma; the smoking is a major modifiable trigger that must be addressed with compassion and cessation support, not shame, or he disengages. Assess and safety-net current severity, give a written action plan with explicit escalation criteria, and arrange a technique check and review.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG245 (2024, joint with BTS and SIGN) · BTS/SIGN 158 (2019) acute asthma · NICE NG209
knowledge.summary: Wheeze only with colds and no symptoms in between, at age 2, fits episodic viral wheeze. Asthma cannot be confirmed by objective tests under 5, and a regular preventer is not the automatic answer. Technique, a written plan and a smoke-free home are the key interventions.

points.t: Episodic viral wheeze: wheeze and cough only with colds, well between episodes. Asthma becomes more likely with interval symptoms (night cough, wheeze with play or laughing when well), atopy such as eczema or allergic rhinitis, or frequent severe episodes.

For children under 5 with suspected asthma, NICE NG245 advises treating on clinical judgement and reviewing regularly; objective tests are attempted once the child reaches 5. An 8 to 12 week trial of twice-daily paediatric low-dose ICS is considered when symptoms suggest a need for maintenance therapy or there are severe acute episodes.

BTS/SIGN 158 (2019): an inhaled beta-2 agonist through a pressurised inhaler and spacer is the preferred option for mild to moderate acute wheeze in children. Give one puff at a time into the spacer with tidal breathing. Dose per BNFC and the written plan.

A toddler needs an age-appropriate face mask sealed over nose and mouth. Several puffs sprayed at once, a poor seal or no spacer are common reasons for apparent treatment failure. Watch the parent demonstrate.

NICE NG209: give clear advice about the dangers of second-hand smoke, recommend not smoking in the home or around children, offer very brief advice on stopping and refer to local stop-smoking support.

Urgent or emergency review for marked recession, difficulty feeding or talking, exhaustion or drowsiness, cyanosis, or a reliever that does not help or does not last. Severity cannot be fully judged by phone — convert to a face-to-face review if in doubt.

dg.d: Open question; heard all three of his questions (asthma, preventer, technique) and agreed to cover them.
Household smoking, his own frightening childhood asthma, the cousin on a preventer, and managing a wriggling toddler.
Severity assessed by phone through the parent; face-to-face review if uncertain; technique demonstration with the nurse.
Episodic viral wheeze vs suspected asthma (interval symptoms, atopy), with severity of the current episode.
Checked recession, feeding, alertness and reliever response; knows the features needing emergency care.
Explained episodic viral wheeze in plain words and why an asthma label is not applied yet.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Salbutamol via spacer and mask with correct technique; no reflex preventer; clear criteria for an ICS trial (NICE NG245).
Smoking addressed without shame and stop-smoking referral agreed (NICE NG209).
Written action plan, 999 triggers, nurse technique check this week, review if interval symptoms appear.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “not sure I’m getting it into him” and the smoking guilt, and explored both.
Idea (asthma like his cousin), concern (it’s his fault; his own asthma), expectation (a brown preventer).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.

ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — guilt about his smoking contributing (and feeling judged), plus anxiety from his own frightening childhood asthma; hoping a preventer inhaler fixes it instead of facing the smoking — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Lee calling about Reuben. Can I just check I’m speaking to his dad, and is he with you now? Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Confirms identity and opens with an open question

model.text: Yes, he’s here. Every cold he goes wheezy and chesty — fourth time this winter. A&E gave him the blue inhaler last time and it helped. Has he got asthma? My sister’s lad is on a brown preventer. And honestly, I’m not sure I’m even getting the inhaler into him.

Three good questions — is it asthma, does he need a preventer, and the inhaler itself. I’ll make sure we cover all three. First I want to check how he is right now, then we’ll go through the rest. Is that okay?
model.why: Reflects his agenda back and prioritises current safety

model.text: Yeah, fine.
Can you look at him for me now? Is he playing and chatting? Is he drinking? And if you lift his top, is the skin between or under his ribs sucking in when he breathes?
model.why: Assesses current severity by phone using what the parent can see

model.text: He’s playing and chatting away. Eating and drinking okay. Bit wheezy, but his ribs aren’t sucking in, no.
Good. And when you give the blue inhaler, how long does it help for?
It helps — he picks up after it.
When he hasn’t got a cold, is he completely well? Any coughing at night, or wheezing when he runs about or laughs? Any eczema or hay fever?
model.why: Separates episodic viral wheeze from interval symptoms and atopy

model.text: No, between colds he’s totally fine.
Talk me through exactly how you give the inhaler — what do you do, step by step?
model.why: Explores the technique problem he flagged

model.text: I shake it, put it in the spacer, press it a few times and try to hold the mask on. He fights it and wriggles off.
You mentioned your sister’s little boy. What were you hoping we’d decide today?
model.why: Elicits expectation behind the preventer request

model.text: I suppose a preventer, so it stops. I had asthma as a kid and it was scary. And… I smoke. I go outside, but I know. I keep thinking maybe it’s me.

Thank you for telling me that — it can’t have been easy. It makes sense you’re watchful when you remember how frightening your own asthma was. And going outside to smoke shows how much you’re already trying to protect him.
model.why: Acknowledges fear and guilt without shaming

model.text: I just feel like I’m getting it wrong.

You’re not. What you describe — wheezy only with colds, completely well in between — is what we call viral wheeze. His airways are small, so colds go to his chest. Many children grow out of it as their airways grow. At two, we can’t test for asthma properly, and with nothing in between colds, a daily preventer isn’t usually the answer.
model.why: Distinguishes viral wheeze from asthma and explains the preventer decision

model.text: So not a brown one.

Not for now. If he starts coughing at night or wheezing between colds, or the episodes get severe, we’d think again and might try one for a couple of months. What will help most today is the inhaler technique you mentioned.
model.why: Gives a conditional plan with clear criteria to revisit

model.text: Here’s the trick. One puff into the spacer at a time — not several. Hold the mask gently but firmly over his nose and mouth so there’s a seal, and let him breathe normally in and out several times. Then the next puff. Crying doesn’t help the medicine get in, so a cuddle on your lap, or while he’s calm, works best.
model.why: Coaches spacer and mask technique in plain words

model.text: One at a time. I didn’t know that — I’ve been doing a few in one go.

Can I raise the smoking gently? Smoke on clothes, hair and breath still reaches him, even when you’re outside, and it’s one of the biggest triggers for these chests. Stopping would help him more than any inhaler. Our local stop-smoking service gives medicines and support, which makes quitting much more likely to work. Would you like me to refer you?
model.why: Addresses smoking as a modifiable trigger without shame and offers referral

model.text: …Yeah. I’ve been meaning to. Go on.

Great. I’ll also send you a written plan: when to give the blue inhaler, how many puffs, and when to get help. And I’d like our nurse to watch you do the inhaler this week, so you feel confident. How does that sound?
model.why: Shared plan with a written action plan and technique check

model.text: That’d help. I just want to know I’m doing it right.

Right now he sounds mild. Call 999 if he’s working hard to breathe with his ribs sucking in, can’t drink or talk, is unusually sleepy, or his lips look blue. Ring us the same day if the blue inhaler isn’t helping or he’s needing it more and more.
Before you go, tell me back how you’ll give the inhaler tonight.
Shake it, into the spacer, mask on tight, one puff, let him breathe a few times, then the next. And ring 999 if his ribs suck in or he goes sleepy or blue.
Perfect. Nurse appointment this week, smoking referral today, written plan by text. You’re doing a good job, and this will make it easier.
model.why: Summarises actions and closes with encouragement

social.t: Smoking outside reduces but does not remove exposure; smoke on clothes and breath still matters. Parental guilt is common and drives avoidance, so the topic needs compassion.
A parent’s own frightening childhood asthma, and a relative’s child on a preventer, shape expectations. A written plan replaces guesswork at night.

legal.t: In England it is illegal to smoke in a private vehicle carrying anyone under 18 (Smoke-free (Private Vehicles) Regulations 2015). Worth mentioning if the family drives.

professional.t: A telephone assessment of a wheezy toddler relies on what the parent can see. Document the features checked and convert to face-to-face review if there is any doubt (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: recognise the limits of the consultation).
An asthma code at 2 without objective testing can follow a child for years. Record “episodic viral wheeze” or “suspected asthma” accurately, with a plan to review at 5 (NICE NG245).

community.t: Local stop-smoking service; practice nurse or community pharmacy inhaler technique check; Asthma and Lung UK written action plans and technique videos for parents.

redFlags: Recession, tracheal tug, difficulty feeding or talking, drowsiness, cyanosis — emergency care
Reliever not helping, or needed more and more — same-day review
Interval symptoms or atopy — rethink the diagnosis (suspected asthma, NICE NG245)
psychosocial: Father smokes, tries to smoke outside, and feels guilty
His own childhood asthma was frightening
A wriggling toddler who fights the mask
ice: Idea: “He’s got asthma, like my sister’s lad.”
Concern: that his smoking is causing it, and memories of his own asthma

playbook.diagnosis: Episodic viral-induced wheeze in a 2-year-old: wheeze only with colds, well between episodes, no interval symptoms, currently mild. Not labelled asthma at this age; review if interval symptoms or severe episodes develop.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Reuben has small airways, so when he gets a cold it goes to his chest and makes him wheezy. That’s called viral wheeze. It isn’t the same as asthma, and many children grow out of it as they get bigger.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked about a preventer because you want this to stop, and because your own asthma frightened you. Let’s do the things that will actually help most right now.”
management.psychosocial: Raise smoking with compassion, acknowledge the effort of smoking outside, offer referral to stop-smoking support; involve him as the expert in his own child’s care.
sharedPlan: Salbutamol via spacer and mask, one puff at a time with tidal breathing (BTS/SIGN 158, 2019); dose per BNFC and the written plan
No regular preventer for now; consider an 8 to 12 week ICS trial if interval symptoms or severe episodes (NICE NG245)
Stop-smoking referral (NICE NG209); nurse technique check this week
safetyNet: 999 for recession, unable to drink or talk, drowsiness or blue lips
Same-day contact if the reliever isn’t helping; review if symptoms appear between colds

pitfalls.intro: This station is rarely failed on the diagnosis. It is failed by giving the preventer on request, by skipping the technique problem the father flagged, and by handling the smoking in a way that makes him switch off.

items.fail: Starting a regular inhaled steroid because the father asked and the cousin has one.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Pure episodic viral wheeze is not an automatic indication; NICE NG245 reserves an ICS trial for suspected asthma with persistent or severe features.
items.fix: Explain viral wheeze, say “not for now”, and give the specific signs that would change that.

items.fail: Discussing the diagnosis without first checking how Reuben is right now.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” A telephone call about a wheezy toddler must establish current severity.
items.fix: Ask the father to look: playing, drinking, ribs sucking in, reliever response.

items.fail: Hearing “I’m not sure I’m getting it into him” and moving on.
items.why: Poor technique is the likeliest reason the reliever seems to fail, and he raised it himself.
items.fix: Ask him to describe each step, then coach one puff at a time with a sealed mask and tidal breathing.

items.fail: “You need to stop smoking, it’s making him ill.”
items.why: Shaming is flagged as judgemental; he disengages from the whole plan.
items.fix: Credit his effort to smoke outside, explain third-hand smoke simply, and offer referral as help, not a verdict.

items.fail: Missing the father’s own childhood asthma when he mentions it.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” It explains his anxiety and his wish for a preventer.
items.fix: “It makes sense you’re watchful — your own asthma sounds frightening.” Then show how the plan removes the guesswork.

items.fail: Ending with “ring back if he gets worse”, with no written plan or named symptoms.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing feedback statement.
items.fix: Written action plan, named 999 features, nurse technique check this week, and a teach-back.

timeMap.d: He brings three questions: asthma, preventer, technique. Name all three and say you’ll check how Reuben is first.
Ask the father to look: playing, drinking, recession. Reliever response. Interval symptoms, atopy. How he gives the inhaler, step by step.
Why a preventer matters to him: his own childhood asthma and the smoking. Respond with warmth before any advice.
Viral wheeze vs asthma; not a preventer for now, with criteria to revisit. Coach one-puff-at-a-time technique. Raise smoking kindly and offer referral.
Written plan, 999 triggers, nurse technique check. Teach-back of the technique.

wordPics.fail: Labels asthma and starts a preventer on request, or dismisses it as “just a cold”; never checks current severity; ignores the technique problem; lectures about smoking or avoids it; no written plan or safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Assesses severity by phone; explains viral wheeze and why a preventer is not automatic; corrects spacer technique; mentions smoking and offers support; gives basic safety-netting.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: hears the guilt and his own childhood fear and responds before advising; gives clear criteria for when a preventer would be tried; coaches technique so well he can teach it back; gains his agreement to a stop-smoking referral; written plan and nurse check booked.

avoid.dont: “Yes, it sounds like asthma — I’ll start a brown inhaler.”
avoid.instead: “Wheezy only with colds and fine in between is viral wheeze. A daily preventer isn’t usually the answer for that at his age.”
avoid.why: A reflex label and preventer is not in line with NICE NG245 for this pattern.

avoid.dont: “You need to stop smoking — it’s causing his wheeze.”
avoid.instead: “Going outside shows you’re already trying. Smoke on clothes still reaches him, and stopping would help his chest more than any inhaler. Can I help?”
avoid.why: Blame makes him disengage; compassion and an offer of support get a referral.

avoid.dont: “Just give him a few puffs when he’s wheezy.”
avoid.instead: “One puff into the spacer at a time, mask sealed, let him breathe normally several times, then the next.”
avoid.why: Vague instructions leave the actual problem — poor technique — untouched.

SCA_MODELS.text: I just feel like I’m getting it wrong.

You’re not. What you describe — wheezy only with colds, completely well in between — is what we call viral wheeze. His airways are small, so colds go to his chest. Many children grow out of it as their airways grow. At two, we can’t test for asthma properly, and with nothing in between colds, a daily preventer isn’t usually the answer.
SCA_MODELS.why: Distinguishes viral wheeze from asthma and explains the preventer decision

SCA_MODELS.text: So not a brown one.

Not for now. If he starts coughing at night or wheezing between colds, or the episodes get severe, we’d think again and might try one for a couple of months. What will help most today is the inhaler technique you mentioned.
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives a conditional plan with clear criteria to revisit

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s the trick. One puff into the spacer at a time — not several. Hold the mask gently but firmly over his nose and mouth so there’s a seal, and let him breathe normally in and out several times. Then the next puff. Crying doesn’t help the medicine get in, so a cuddle on your lap, or while he’s calm, works best.
SCA_MODELS.why: Coaches spacer and mask technique in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: One at a time. I didn’t know that — I’ve been doing a few in one go.

Can I raise the smoking gently? Smoke on clothes, hair and breath still reaches him, even when you’re outside, and it’s one of the biggest triggers for these chests. Stopping would help him more than any inhaler. Our local stop-smoking service gives medicines and support, which makes quitting much more likely to work. Would you like me to refer you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses smoking as a modifiable trigger without shame and offers referral

SCA_MODELS.text: …Yeah. I’ve been meaning to. Go on.

Great. I’ll also send you a written plan: when to give the blue inhaler, how many puffs, and when to get help. And I’d like our nurse to watch you do the inhaler this week, so you feel confident. How does that sound?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shared plan with a written action plan and technique check

SCA_MODELS.text: That’d help. I just want to know I’m doing it right.

Right now he sounds mild. Call 999 if he’s working hard to breathe with his ribs sucking in, can’t drink or talk, is unusually sleepy, or his lips look blue. Ring us the same day if the blue inhaler isn’t helping or he’s needing it more and more.
Before you go, tell me back how you’ll give the inhaler tonight.
Shake it, into the spacer, mask on tight, one puff, let him breathe a few times, then the next. And ring 999 if his ribs suck in or he goes sleepy or blue.
Perfect. Nurse appointment this week, smoking referral today, written plan by text. You’re doing a good job, and this will make it easier.
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises actions and closes with encouragement

SCA_STEM.name: Reuben
pmh: Recurrent wheeze with viral colds — fourth episode this winter
meds: Salbutamol inhaler with spacer and mask (given after A&E attendance)
SCA_STEM.recent: A&E attendance with the last episode: wheeze treated with salbutamol, discharged. Household: father smokes (reports smoking outside).
SCA_STEM.reason: Father has booked a telephone call: wheezy again with a cold, and asking whether Reuben has asthma and needs a preventer.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG245 (2024, joint with BTS and SIGN) · BTS/SIGN 158 (2019) acute asthma · NICE NG209
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Wheeze only with colds and no symptoms in between, at age 2, fits episodic viral wheeze. Asthma cannot be confirmed by objective tests under 5, and a regular preventer is not the automatic answer. Technique, a written plan and a smoke-free home are the key interventions.

points.t: Episodic viral wheeze: wheeze and cough only with colds, well between episodes. Asthma becomes more likely with interval symptoms (night cough, wheeze with play or laughing when well), atopy such as eczema or allergic rhinitis, or frequent severe episodes.

For children under 5 with suspected asthma, NICE NG245 advises treating on clinical judgement and reviewing regularly; objective tests are attempted once the child reaches 5. An 8 to 12 week trial of twice-daily paediatric low-dose ICS is considered when symptoms suggest a need for maintenance therapy or there are severe acute episodes.

BTS/SIGN 158 (2019): an inhaled beta-2 agonist through a pressurised inhaler and spacer is the preferred option for mild to moderate acute wheeze in children. Give one puff at a time into the spacer with tidal breathing. Dose per BNFC and the written plan.

A toddler needs an age-appropriate face mask sealed over nose and mouth. Several puffs sprayed at once, a poor seal or no spacer are common reasons for apparent treatment failure. Watch the parent demonstrate.

NICE NG209: give clear advice about the dangers of second-hand smoke, recommend not smoking in the home or around children, offer very brief advice on stopping and refer to local stop-smoking support.

Urgent or emergency review for marked recession, difficulty feeding or talking, exhaustion or drowsiness, cyanosis, or a reliever that does not help or does not last. Severity cannot be fully judged by phone — convert to a face-to-face review if in doubt.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; heard all three of his questions (asthma, preventer, technique) and agreed to cover them.
Household smoking, his own frightening childhood asthma, the cousin on a preventer, and managing a wriggling toddler.
Picked up “not sure I’m getting it into him” and the smoking guilt, and explored both.
Idea (asthma like his cousin), concern (it’s his fault; his own asthma), expectation (a brown preventer).
Severity assessed by phone through the parent; face-to-face review if uncertain; technique demonstration with the nurse.
Episodic viral wheeze vs suspected asthma (interval symptoms, atopy), with severity of the current episode.
Checked recession, feeding, alertness and reliever response; knows the features needing emergency care.
Explained episodic viral wheeze in plain words and why an asthma label is not applied yet.
Salbutamol via spacer and mask with correct technique; no reflex preventer; clear criteria for an ICS trial (NICE NG245).
Smoking addressed without shame and stop-smoking referral agreed (NICE NG209).
Written action plan, 999 triggers, nurse technique check this week, review if interval symptoms appear.

social.t: Smoking outside reduces but does not remove exposure; smoke on clothes and breath still matters. Parental guilt is common and drives avoidance, so the topic needs compassion.
A parent’s own frightening childhood asthma, and a relative’s child on a preventer, shape expectations. A written plan replaces guesswork at night.

legal.t: In England it is illegal to smoke in a private vehicle carrying anyone under 18 (Smoke-free (Private Vehicles) Regulations 2015). Worth mentioning if the family drives.

professional.t: A telephone assessment of a wheezy toddler relies on what the parent can see. Document the features checked and convert to face-to-face review if there is any doubt (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: recognise the limits of the consultation).
An asthma code at 2 without objective testing can follow a child for years. Record “episodic viral wheeze” or “suspected asthma” accurately, with a plan to review at 5 (NICE NG245).

community.t: Local stop-smoking service; practice nurse or community pharmacy inhaler technique check; Asthma and Lung UK written action plans and technique videos for parents.

redFlags: Recession, tracheal tug, difficulty feeding or talking, drowsiness, cyanosis — emergency care
Reliever not helping, or needed more and more — same-day review
Interval symptoms or atopy — rethink the diagnosis (suspected asthma, NICE NG245)

A wriggling toddler who fights the mask
ice: Idea: “He’s got asthma, like my sister’s lad.”
Concern: that his smoking is causing it, and memories of his own asthma

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Episodic viral-induced wheeze in a 2-year-old: wheeze only with colds, well between episodes, no interval symptoms, currently mild. Not labelled asthma at this age; review if interval symptoms or severe episodes develop.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Reuben has small airways, so when he gets a cold it goes to his chest and makes him wheezy. That’s called viral wheeze. It isn’t the same as asthma, and many children grow out of it as they get bigger.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked about a preventer because you want this to stop, and because your own asthma frightened you. Let’s do the things that will actually help most right now.”
management.psychosocial: Raise smoking with compassion, acknowledge the effort of smoking outside, offer referral to stop-smoking support; involve him as the expert in his own child’s care.

No regular preventer for now; consider an 8 to 12 week ICS trial if interval symptoms or severe episodes (NICE NG245)
Stop-smoking referral (NICE NG209); nurse technique check this week

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is rarely failed on the diagnosis. It is failed by giving the preventer on request, by skipping the technique problem the father flagged, and by handling the smoking in a way that makes him switch off.

items.fail: Starting a regular inhaled steroid because the father asked and the cousin has one.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Pure episodic viral wheeze is not an automatic indication; NICE NG245 reserves an ICS trial for suspected asthma with persistent or severe features.
items.fix: Explain viral wheeze, say “not for now”, and give the specific signs that would change that.

items.fail: Discussing the diagnosis without first checking how Reuben is right now.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” A telephone call about a wheezy toddler must establish current severity.
items.fix: Ask the father to look: playing, drinking, ribs sucking in, reliever response.

items.fail: Hearing “I’m not sure I’m getting it into him” and moving on.
items.why: Poor technique is the likeliest reason the reliever seems to fail, and he raised it himself.
items.fix: Ask him to describe each step, then coach one puff at a time with a sealed mask and tidal breathing.

items.fail: “You need to stop smoking, it’s making him ill.”
items.why: Shaming is flagged as judgemental; he disengages from the whole plan.
items.fix: Credit his effort to smoke outside, explain third-hand smoke simply, and offer referral as help, not a verdict.

items.fail: Missing the father’s own childhood asthma when he mentions it.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” It explains his anxiety and his wish for a preventer.
items.fix: “It makes sense you’re watchful — your own asthma sounds frightening.” Then show how the plan removes the guesswork.

items.fail: Ending with “ring back if he gets worse”, with no written plan or named symptoms.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing feedback statement.
items.fix: Written action plan, named 999 features, nurse technique check this week, and a teach-back.
